description: We are Unsolved Loop, a team passionate about space, technology, and problem-solving. Our project, LunarWindow, is an interactive tool for comparing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates. It visualizes Sun and Earth visibility relative to the local terrain horizon, helping users understand lighting conditions and direct-to-Earth visibility. We’re looking for teammates interested in astronomy, Python, data, geospatial technology, web development, UI/UX, research, or technical communication.
summary: LightPath is a browser-based planning prototype for the lunar south pole, where terrain decides when the Sun and Earth are visible. It combines NASA SPICE geometry (checked against JPL Horizons), NASA LOLA terrain and a space-time route solver to show when each body clears the local horizon, how much of its disc is visible, and whether a rover can reach a goal before light or the Earth link is lost. Outputs: departure-window maps, uncertainty margins from NASA's terrain error map, evidence cards with checksums, and open CSV/Parquet/calendar exports. Our Trust page publishes every test result, including two checks not yet run. Terrain is real LOLA at one test location, not a mission site. Why it matters: early CLPS and surface-operations planning depends on sunlight and communication windows that terrain controls to fractions of a degree, so planners need tools that state their geometry, uncertainty and limits openly.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LightPath answers a question every lunar landing has to settle early: where, and when, will a lander or rover have sunlight and a line of sight to Earth?

Near the Moon's south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.5 degrees above the horizon, and Earth sits only a few degrees up. A 100 m ridge 10 km away rises about 0.41 degrees on a spherical Moon, enough to hide the Sun completely. So terrain, not only orbital geometry, decides whether a site is usable.

For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, LightPath lets you pick a site and a date range and see, hour by hour, when the Sun and Earth are above the local terrain horizon and how much of each disc is visible. It then goes one step further: it asks whether a rover can travel from the landing point to a goal before the light or the Earth link disappears.

HOW IT WORKS

Geometry: Sun and Earth directions come from NASA's SPICE toolkit and kernels (DE421), calculated from the exact point on the surface using that point's own local vertical.

Terrain: we use NASA's LOLA elevation models (20 m near the site, 80 m farther out) and trace the horizon in every direction, including the Moon's curvature.

Visibility: the Sun is half a degree wide and Earth about two, so a ridge often covers only part of them. We compute the visible fraction of each disc, not just yes or no. We also check whether a Deep Space Network station can see the Moon at the same time (the station list is marked unverified in the app).

Uncertainty: NASA publishes an error map for the terrain. We used it to set a 0.03 degree safety margin and to label results robustly visible, marginal or blocked.

Route planning: a space-time route planner runs in the browser. It finds the earliest and latest departure that works, and when no route exists it says which constraint blocks it and the smallest change that would fix it.

Evidence: every result comes with a checksummed record of the data and kernels behind it, and exports to CSV, Parquet and calendar files.

WHAT WE FOUND AT OUR DEMONSTRATION LOCATION

This is real LOLA terrain at latitude -89.5, longitude 0, a test location and not a mission site, over 1 to 30 November 2026 at 30-minute steps, with a 2 m mast. The skyline peaks at +9.6 degrees. The Sun is at least half visible 22.7 percent of the time, Earth 36.4 percent, and Sun plus ground-station contact 15.1 percent. The longest dark spell is 556.5 hours. In our demonstration traverse (1.2 km at 0.05 m/s, about 6.7 hours), leaving in the first 4.5 hours works; leaving later fails because a moving shadow closes the corridor.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

Most of our effort went into getting the numbers right, and the app shows the results on a Trust page. Flat-sphere and wall-ridge horizon calculations match closed-form answers. Our Sun and Earth directions agree with NASA's JPL Horizons system to within [0.00004] degrees at two test locations [CONFIRM after rerun]. The route solver matches an exhaustive search on 300 random cases. Our first, approximate Sun and Earth model turned out to be wrong by tens of degrees when checked against an independent source, so we replaced it with SPICE and added tests so that cannot happen again. Two checks are not done yet and are marked NOT RUN: a comparison with a published NASA illumination result, and an independent open tool.

WHY IT MATTERS

Planning a landing or a traverse near the pole depends on sunlight and communication windows that terrain controls to fractions of a degree. LightPath gives planners, students and mission teams an open tool that shows its geometry, its uncertainty and its limits, so the answer can be checked rather than trusted.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Most tools stop at when a site is lit. We treat light and the Earth link as constraints that change over time and ask whether a rover can complete a route inside them. The departure-window map turns a solver into a decision tool, a true-scale lens shows partial visibility honestly, and the uncertainty margin comes from NASA's own error map. We also show what we have not verified.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We matched the kernels to the terrain's reference frame, used directions measured from the surface rather than the Moon's centre (a difference of up to 0.26 degrees for Earth), allowed for the tilt of local vertical over a traverse (about 0.033 degrees per kilometre), treated the 20 m terrain resolution as a limit on mast-height claims, and used 30-minute time steps with conservative checks so a route is not credited with light that disappears mid-move.

TOOLS

Python 3.11 (NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, pyproj, SpiceyPy, PyArrow) for the data pipeline; TypeScript, React and Vite for the browser app; Web Workers for the route solver; GitHub Actions and automated Python, web and end-to-end tests. No special hardware.

LIMITS

This is a prototype for planning and education, not for flight. Sun visibility is not electrical power and Earth visibility is not a link budget. Terrain is real at one test location, and the mission browser holds example entries only. The 20 m terrain does not resolve rocks or small craters, and the rover speed and slope limit are assumptions.

AI ASSISTANCE

We used AI tools to help write code, and documentation: Claude from Anthropic. No AI-generated images, audio or video are used in the project.

Source code: https://github.com/AnmolGarg8/LightPath
